title: States of Matter
hook: Solid, liquid, gas, plasma — the difference is how tightly particles are bound. Add heat and matter changes state, but during the change the temperature holds still.
key_points: Solid, liquid, gas, and plasma differ in how tightly particles bind and how freely they move.
Adding or removing heat drives phase changes: melting, boiling, freezing.
During a phase change the temperature stays steady — heat goes into breaking or forming bonds.
That latent heat is why boiling water holds near 100 C until it's all steam.
content_html: Most matter shows up as a solid, a liquid, or a gas — and there's a fourth common state, plasma, where the gas is so hot its particles tear apart into charged pieces. What separates them is simple: how tightly the particles are locked together and how freely they roam. In a solid they're held in fixed positions; in a liquid they slide past one another; in a gas they fly apart and fill whatever space they're given.
extra_html: Move between states by adding or removing heat — melting, boiling, freezing, condensing. Here's the surprising part: while a substance is actually changing state, its temperature doesn't budge. The energy you pour in goes entirely into breaking the bonds that hold particles together, not into making them move faster. That hidden energy is called latent heat, and it's why a pot of boiling water sits stubbornly near 100 C until the last of it has turned to steam. Wikipedia's article on states of matter covers the states and the energetics of changing between them.

related.title: Heat vs. Temperature
related.hook: A sparkler can hit thousands of degrees yet barely burn you — because temperature and heat are not the same thing.

related.title: Three Ways Heat Moves
related.hook: Heat travels three ways: conduction through contact, convection by circulating fluid, and radiation across empty space. Most warming you feel mixes all three.

flashcards.prompt: What basically distinguishes a solid, a liquid, and a gas?
flashcards.back_html: How tightly the particles are bound and how freely they move: rigidly held in a solid, loosely flowing in a liquid, and spread far apart and free in a gas.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the temperature of boiling water stay near 100 C even as you keep heating it?

choices.text: The added heat goes into breaking bonds (latent heat), not raising temperature
Water cannot get any hotter than 100 C under any conditions
The stove automatically stops adding heat

flashcards.explanation_html: During the liquid-to-gas change, incoming energy is spent pulling molecules apart rather than speeding them up, so the temperature holds steady.

flashcards.prompt: What drives a substance to change from one state to another?
flashcards.explanation_html: Adding heat melts or boils a substance; removing heat freezes or condenses it — phase changes are driven by gaining or losing energy.
